title: The Impact of the Mariel Boatlift on the Miami Labor Market
research_question: How does a large, sudden influx of relatively unskilled immigrants into a single city affect the wages and unemployment rates of less-skilled native workers, and does it also affect the labor market outcomes of earlier immigrants from the same origin already residing in that city?
data_description: The analysis uses individual-level micro-data from the merged outgoing rotation group samples of the Current Population Survey (CPS) for 1979-1985, with the Miami metropolitan area sample averaging roughly 1,200 individuals per month. Additional data come from the 1980 Decennial Census (conducted April 1, 1980) for a pre-treatment snapshot of the Miami labor market, and the March 1985 CPS Mobility Supplement, which identifies recent Cuban arrivals via residence five years prior. The unit of observation is a working-age individual (16-61). Key variables include hourly earnings (deflated by the CPI), employment status, unemployment, labor force participation, education, potential experience, gender, ethnicity (white non-Hispanic, black non-Hispanic, Cuban, other Hispanic), occupation, and industry. Comparison cities used are Atlanta, Los Angeles, Houston, and Tampa-St. Petersburg, chosen for similar demographic composition and employment growth trajectories.
institutional_context: Following Fidel Castro's April 20, 1980 declaration that Cubans wishing to emigrate could leave from the port of Mariel, approximately 125,000 Cuban refugees arrived in the United States via a privately chartered flotilla between May and September 1980. About half settled permanently in Miami, raising the city's labor force by roughly 7% and increasing the number of Cuban workers in Miami by about 20%. The Mariel immigrants (Mariels) were on average less educated, younger, and more concentrated in laborer and service occupations than earlier Cuban arrivals, and many had limited English proficiency. Miami at the time was the most immigrant-intensive city in the U.S., with a substantial pre-existing Cuban enclave, a sizable black population, and an industry mix (notably textiles and apparel) historically reliant on unskilled labor. The unanticipated, politically driven nature and concentrated timing of the inflow provide an exogenous supply shock to one local labor market.
